title: Manage IT user identity and authorization
goal: Every person and agent role has its own identity on every system, holds only the scopes its work used, authenticates with a second factor where the system can move money, change DNS, push code or read customer data, and every change of access is recorded with its date and who approved it.

steps.do: Write the one identity rule the venture follows (one identity per person and per agent role, never shared, access granted for a named activity and removed when it ends) and check that each system can actually express it, naming the systems that cannot.

Keep on the connection records the current list of who exists on each system: every person, every agent role, every specialist and every leftover account nobody claims, with the date each was last checked.
Compare each holder's scopes with the activities its work actually performed, remove what was not used, and prepare every widening as a decision for the founder with what it would reach.

Check how each account proves who it is and record it: a second factor on every account that can move money, change DNS, push code or read customer data, and, where the venture has more than a couple of people, whether one sign-in could cover several systems instead of separate passwords; propose turning a second factor on, and leave buying single sign-on to the founder.
On a date, read each system's own access settings rather than the venture's record of them, write where the two disagree, and correct the record.

When a credential may have leaked or an account may have been used by someone else, write the timeline from the provider's own logs, revoke and rotate what is yours to revoke, name what the credential could have reached, and tell the founder at once; the founder decides what is said to anyone outside and whether data is deleted.

consider.why: There is nothing to respond to until a leak or an unexpected sign-in is reported.
consider.when: A provider has reported an unexpected sign-in, a secret has appeared in the open, or someone reports a lost device.

steps.do: Prepare for the founder what a test would cover, what it must never touch and what it would cost, and leave hiring the tester and giving permission to the founder; you never test a provider's system and never attack anything.

consider.why: A paid test is worth money only once the venture runs its own exposed application with real customer data.
consider.when: The venture runs its own internet-facing application holding customer data, or a customer requires a test.

steps.do: Check the joins between systems (a sign-in that grants access to another system, a token one service holds for another, an agent credential reused across two systems) and write what each join would let through if the first system were taken over.

consider.why: A join between systems turns one compromised account into several, and matters once two systems trust each other.
consider.when: One system grants access to another, or a service holds a token for another.

steps.do: Record every removal, every rotation and every disagreement found as evidence on the decision it bears on, propose the order of access fixes to the product lead, and raise every widening for the founder with what it would reach.

done_criteria.check: Does every person and agent role hold its own identity with no scope its work did not use, is a second factor on or open as a decision for every account that can move money, change DNS, push code or read customer data, and was every widening approved by the founder?
